newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi confident Italy will be in EMU.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi confident Italy will be in EMU.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in an interview published on Friday he had no doubt Italy would be among the founder members of the single European currency and that the country's economic recovery was at hand.

"Without a doubt we will enter (EMU)," Prodi said in an interview in Milan's Corriere della Sera in response to a question if Italy would be part of European economic and monetary union (EMU) or be left out.
The interview was published a day before the first anniversary of the birth of Prodi's government -- Italy's 55th since World War Two.

Last week EU finance ministers in Brussels approved a sharply worded Commission report on the state of Italy's finances, suggesting that many of the measures taken recently to cut the budget deficit were not sustainable.
The EU finance ministers criticised Italy for lax controls on state spending in 1996 and told Rome it still had much to do if it wanted to reduce its budget deficit in a lasting fashion.
Prodi said Brussels' report was not the end of the road for Italy. "There was no examination and no failing vote," he said.

"The real test for Italy's place in EMU will be next spring," Prodi said in a reference to when the final decision will be made on which countries meet the criteria to join the single European currency from the start.
Prodi said the Italian economy was headed for a recovery.
"The period of fat years are not yet here, but we are paving the way for it. The economy is beginning to recover. Let's wait for the budget," he said.

Enrico Giovannini, chief economist of the state statistics institute ISTAT, said this week Italy would see close to zero economic growth in the first quarter of 1997 but that there was some sign of optimism for the second quarter.
The government's official target for 1997 is for 1.2 percent gross domestic product (GDP) growth.
Prodi defended Italy's economic qualifications in Europe.

"Let's be careful (about comparisons with other countries)," he said. "Italy's economy is twice as large as Spain's and I would like to remind you quietly that our per-capita income is greater than Britain's, albeit slightly, and I believe this is no small matter."
The outlines of Italy's latest three-year programme of economic targets, known as the DPEF, is expected to be presented to the cabinet later on Friday by Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi.
The eagerly awaited DPEF is expected to give indications of savings the government hopes to make from a planned reform of the welfare state. It will also give new 1998 deficit forecasts.
Prodi's government, the first to include the former communists, took office on May 17 last year after the Olive Tree coalition won the general elections in April.
It has a comfortable majority in the Senate (upper house) but relies on the hard-left Communist Refoundation party for its majority in the Chamber of Deputies.
The opposition centre-right of former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi says the small Marxist party enjoys disproportionate power over the coalition, particularly on economic issues.

Asked if Communist Refoundation, which is opposed to social spending cuts in order to reduce the deficit, had conditioned the government, Prodi said: "They have slowed us down but I think that (even without them) certain changes should be carried out slowly and with agreement by everyone."
